title: Building STRIKEWISE: Engineering an Options Pricing Engine with Python and SciPy
author: NandanDivate
summary: Options trading involves more than predicting whether an underlying index will move up or down. A change in the underlying price, implied volatility, interest rates, and time to expiry can all affect an option's theoretical premium. I wanted to build a project that explored these relationships mathematically while also applying practical software engineering concepts. That led me to build STRIKEWISE, an open-source quantitative options pricing and risk engine focused on NIFTY 50 options. GitHub: https://github.com/NandanDivate/STRIKEWISE Live API: https://strikewise-4mxr.onrender.com/docs The problem I wanted to solve Consider this scenario: You hold a NIFTY 24,500 Call option. You want to understand: What could its theoretical premium become if NIFTY reaches 24,700? How might the premium change under different implied volatility assumptions? How much does time decay affect the option? What underlying spot price would be required for the option to reach a particular premium? What would the projected P&L and ROI look like? These questions involve multiple variables. Simply applying a fixed percentage to the current option premium does not capture the relationship between the underlying price, volatility, and time. I built STRIKEWISE to model these relationships using the Black-Scholes-Merton framework. The mathematical foundation: Black-Scholes-Merton At the core of STRIKEWISE is the European Black-Scholes-Merton (BSM) pricing model with continuous dividend yield. The model estimates theoretical Call and Put option premiums using: Underlying spot price (S) Strike price (K) Time to expiry (T) Risk-free interest rate (r) Dividend yield (q) Annualized volatility (σ) The model uses: [ d_1 = \frac{\ln(S/K)+(r-q+\sigma^2/2)T}{\sigma\sqrt{T}} ] [ d_2=d_1-\sigma\sqrt{T} ] The Call and Put prices are calculated as: [ C=Se^{-qT}N(d_1)-Ke^{-rT}N(d_2) ] [ P=Ke^{-rT}N(-d_2)-Se^{-qT}N(-d_1) ] One important implementation decision was using the ACT/365 day-count convention. Instead of treating time to expiry as an approximate number of calendar days divided by 365, STRIKEWISE uses timezone-aware time calculations based on elapsed seconds. This helps account for intraday time differences and calendar transitions. Analytical Greeks: Understanding price sensitivity Calculating an option premium is only one part of the problem. I also implemented five analytical Greeks to understand how the theoretical premium responds to changes in different market variables. Greek| What it measures Delta| Sensitivity to underlying price Gamma| Rate of change of Delta Theta| Time decay per calendar day Vega| Sensitivity to a 1 percentage-point IV change Rho| Sensitivity to a 1 percentage-point interest-rate change An important implementation detail was documenting the units consistently. For example: Theta is expressed per calendar day. Vega represents the premium change for a 1 percentage-point implied volatility shift. Rho represents the premium change for a 1 percentage-point interest-rate shift. This avoids ambiguity when interpreting the results. Reverse-solving the underlying price using Brent's method One of the more interesting engineering challenges was implementing an inverse pricing calculation. Most pricing models answer: "What is the theoretical option premium at this underlying spot price?" I also wanted STRIKEWISE to answer: "What underlying spot price is required for the option to reach my target premium?" This is a numerical root-finding problem. I implemented SciPy's Brent root-finding method to solve for the underlying spot price corresponding to a target option premium. The implementation includes dynamic geometric bracketing and handles unattainable targets, including the upper price boundary for Put options. The solver uses a numerical tolerance of (10^{-8}). This was particularly interesting because the problem is not simply about evaluating a formula. It requires finding a valid numerical solution while accounting for the behaviour and limits of the pricing function. Implied volatility scenario analysis Future implied volatility is uncertain. A projected underlying price alone does not tell the entire story because the option premium can change significantly when volatility changes. STRIKEWISE provides three volatility scenarios: Conservative: Current IV minus 2 percentage points. Base: Current IV. Optimistic: Current IV plus 2 percentage points. It also includes automatic lower-bound handling to prevent invalid volatility inputs. These scenarios are assumptions for comparison, not predictions of future volatility. Designing the software architecture I wanted the project to be usable in two different ways: As a reusable Python library. As an asynchronous REST API. To support both, I used a layered modular monolith architecture. The main components are: API Layer FastAPI endpoints. Pydantic v2 request validation. HTTP-level error handling. Service Layer Coordinates pricing calculations. Handles scenario comparisons. Orchestrates time calculations and P&L estimation. Pricing Engine Black-Scholes-Merton implementation. Analytical Greeks. Numerical root solver. Pure mathematical functions. Market Data Layer Abstract provider interface. Offline manual input adapter. DhanHQ API v2 provider adapter. The separation keeps HTTP handling, business orchestration, mathematical calculations, and market data access from becoming tightly coupled. Two ways to use STRIKEWISE Option A: Python library The library can be installed directly from GitHub: pip install git+ https://github.com/NandanDivate/STRIKEWISE.git Example: import strikewise call = strikewise.call_price( spot=24450, strike=24500, time_to_expiry_years=0.05, risk_free_rate=0.07, dividend_yield=0.012, volatility=0.14 ) print(f"Call Premium: ₹{call:.2f}") Greeks can also be calculated directly: greeks = strikewise.calculate_greeks( spot=24450, strike=24500, time_to_expiry_years=0.05, risk_free_rate=0.07, dividend_yield=0.012, volatility=0.14, option_type="CE" ) print("Delta:", greeks.delta) print("Gamma:", greeks.gamma) print("Theta/day:", greeks.theta_per_day) print("Vega:", greeks.vega) print("Rho:", greeks.rho) This allows developers to integrate the pricing engine directly into Python scripts, research workflows, and backtesting systems without making HTTP requests. Option B: FastAPI REST API For developers who prefer HTTP-based integration, STRIKEWISE also exposes its functionality through a REST API. The API supports: Option pricing and estimation. Greeks calculation. Scenario analysis. Target premium calculations. P&L and ROI projections. Interactive documentation is available through Swagger: https://strikewise-4mxr.onrender.com/docs The project is deployed on Render and also supports Docker-based deployment. Testing and validation A mathematical implementation needs more than a few successful example calculations. I added automated unit and integration tests to cover the pricing engine, numerical solver, API workflows, and edge cases. The test run produced: Metric| Result Tests passed| 75 Total statements| 675 Overall coverage| 89% Execution time| 4.27 seconds The coverage report also helped identify modules that need additional testing. For example, the numerical solver currently has lower coverage than the scenario analysis module. That gives me a concrete direction for future improvements. Technology stack Python 3.12 FastAPI SciPy NumPy Pydantic v2 Pytest Docker Render The project is released under the Apache 2.0 license. Limitations and future possibilities STRIKEWISE currently uses the European Black-Scholes-Merton model. That comes with important assumptions and limitations. Theoretical premiums are not guaranteed executable market prices. Actual market prices can differ due to liquidity, bid-ask spreads, market microstructure, and changing volatility. The volatility scenarios are hypothetical assumptions. The engine does not guarantee profitable trades or generate trading signals. There is plenty of room to explore additional pricing models, more market data integrations, and further quantitative risk analysis. Conclusion Building STRIKEWISE gave me an opportunity to work at the intersection of software engineering, numerical methods, and quantitative finance. More importantly, it helped me understand how mathematical models can be translated into reusable software components and accessible APIs. The project is open source, and I would genuinely appreciate technical feedback, suggestions, and contributions. Explore STRIKEWISE: GitHub: https://github.com/NandanDivate/STRIKEWISE Live Swagger API: https://strikewise-4mxr.onrender.com/docs If you work with Python, quantitative finance, derivatives, or numerical computing, I'd be interested in hearing what you think. Disclaimer: STRIKEWISE is an educational and quantitative research project. Its outputs are theoretical estimates based on stated model assumptions, not financial advice or guarantees of market execution or profit. title: Python Virtual Environments Explained: Create and Use venv
author: Lavkush Kumar
summary: Originally published on CodingCush . A Python virtual environment is a private folder that holds its own Python interpreter copy and its own set of installed packages, separate from every other project on your computer. You create one with a single built-in command, python -m venv .venv , activate it, and from then on pip install puts packages into that folder only. In this guide you will learn why environments matter, how to create, activate and rebuild one step by step, and how to fix the problems beginners meet most, with every command tested on Python 3.12. Why Do You Need a Virtual Environment at All? Picture two projects on one laptop. Project A needs version 1 of a library. Project B needs version 2 of the same library. If both projects share one global Python, installing version 2 for Project B can break Project A, and the error will appear days later, in code you did not touch, which is a special kind of frustrating. A virtual environment solves this with simple isolation: one folder per project, one package set per folder. The official venv documentation describes an environment as a directory with its own independent set of packages, created on top of your existing Python installation and isolated from it by default. The tool is called venv , it ships with Python 3.3 and later, and it costs nothing. There is no good reason to skip it, even for small scripts you plan to share. What You Need Before You Start You need Python 3 installed and reachable from your terminal. Check with python --version on Windows or python3 --version on Mac and Linux. If Python is missing, our step-by-step guide to how to install Python on Windows and set up VS Code gets you to a working setup first, including the famous PATH checkbox that everyone forgets once. Step 1: Create the Environment Open a terminal inside your project folder and run: python -m venv .venv On Mac and Linux, use python3 -m venv .venv if python is not available. Let us unpack the command, because every part earns its place. -m tells Python to run a module as a program. venv is the module. .venv is the folder to create; the name is a convention, and the leading dot keeps it quietly out of the way. Python builds the folder with a copy or link of the interpreter, a pip of its own, and a small pyvenv.cfg file that records where the base Python lives. Step 2: Activate It Creating the folder is not enough. You must activate the environment in each new terminal window, so that python and pip point inside the folder: System and shell Activate command Windows, Command Prompt .venv\Scripts\activate.bat Windows, PowerShell .venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1 Mac and Linux, bash or zsh source .venv/bin/activate On Windows PowerShell, if activation is blocked by the execution policy, the official docs suggest allowing local scripts for your user once with Set-ExecutionPolicy -ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned -Scope CurrentUser . When activation works, your prompt gains a (.venv) prefix, like a name badge that says this terminal now works for this project only. Step 3: Prove It Works, Then Install Something Do not trust the name badge alone. Run these two checks (tested on Python 3.12.3): pip --version python -c "import sys; print(sys.prefix != sys.base_prefix)" The first command should report a pip path inside your project's .venv folder, not a system path. The second prints True when Python is genuinely running from a virtual environment, because inside one, sys.prefix points at the environment while sys.base_prefix still points at the base install. Now install packages as usual, for example pip install requests . They land in .venv only. Your other projects will never know. A real venv session run for this article on Python 3.12: after activation, pip reports its path inside the project's .venv folder, and the sys.prefix check prints True, proving the environment is active. Step 4: Save and Rebuild with requirements.txt An environment is disposable by design; the recipe to rebuild it is what you keep. Save the recipe with: pip freeze > requirements.txt That file lists every installed package with its exact version. Commit requirements.txt to Git, and never commit the .venv folder itself; since Python 3.13, venv even writes a starter .gitignore inside the folder to help with exactly that. On a new machine, anyone can rebuild your setup in two lines: python -m venv .venv pip install -r requirements.txt Remember the second line runs after activation. The Python Packaging Authority's guide to pip and virtual environments walks through the same create, activate, install flow if you want a second explanation. And when you finish working, deactivate returns the terminal to the global Python; the folder stays on disk, ready for tomorrow. A Complete Tiny Workflow, Start to Finish mkdir myproject cd myproject python -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate pip install requests pip freeze > requirements.txt deactivate That is the whole habit. It takes under a minute once your fingers learn it, and it quietly prevents the most confusing category of beginner Python bugs: the ones caused by the wrong package version being installed in the wrong place. It also makes helping you much easier: when someone asks what your project needs, you send one small text file instead of a paragraph of guesses, and they can rebuild your exact setup on their own machine and see the same behaviour you see. The habit also pairs well with structuring your code properly; our guide to Python function arguments: positional, keyword, default, args and kwargs is a good next step once your project runs in its own clean environment. Common Mistakes and Troubleshooting Forgetting to activate. The number one issue. You install a package, Python says the module is missing, and the package is sitting happily in the global Python instead. Check for the (.venv) prompt prefix before every pip install . Committing .venv to Git. The folder is large, machine-specific and rebuildable. Commit requirements.txt instead, and add .venv/ to your .gitignore . Moving or renaming the project folder. Environments remember absolute paths, so a moved .venv often breaks. The official advice is simple: delete it and recreate it from requirements.txt . It takes a minute and always works. Two Pythons, one confused terminal. If pip --version shows a path outside .venv after activation, close the terminal, open a fresh one in the project folder and activate again. Stale shells cause most of these mysteries. If errors still mention modules you did install, our guide to Python error handling with try, except and finally helps you read the traceback calmly instead of guessing. Using one environment for everything. That recreates the original problem with extra steps. One project, one environment. Always. Frequently Asked Questions Is venv built into Python, or do I install it? It is built in. The venv module has been part of the standard library since Python 3.3, so python -m venv .venv works on a plain install with nothing extra to download. What should I name my environment? Use .venv . It is the most common convention, editors such as VS Code detect it automatically, and future you will always know what the folder is. Does a virtual environment contain my project code? No. Your code lives in the project folder as usual. The environment folder holds only the interpreter links and installed packages, and you should never place your own files inside it. venv or virtualenv: which should a beginner use? Start with venv. It is built in, well documented and enough for nearly every beginner project. The older third-party virtualenv tool adds a few advanced options you can explore later if you ever need them. Conclusion One command creates the environment, one command activates it, and one small file, requirements.txt , makes the whole setup reproducible anywhere. That tiny routine is the difference between "it works on my machine" as a joke and "it works on my machine" as a promise. Make it the first thing you do in every new Python project, starting with your very next one.

title: Python While Loop!
author: Vinoth
summary: ** Tenali Raman and the Palace Guards** Tenali Raman wishes to meet the King. Before reaching the royal court, he has to pass through many palace gates. A guard is posted at each gate. Every guard demands a share of whatever reward Tenali Raman receives from the King. Tenali Raman agrees and promises: "I will give you half of whatever reward I receive from the King." All the guards allow him to enter. After meeting the King, Tenali Raman receives a reward of 1024 lashes . The interesting question is: How many guards can receive half of the remaining reward until the value becomes less than 1? ##Step 1: Manual Calculation First, we can calculate the result manually. python guard = 0 received_lashes = 1024 guard = 1 received_lashes = received_lashes / 2 guard = 2 received_lashes = received_lashes / 2 guard = 3 received_lashes = received_lashes / 2 guard = 4 received_lashes = received_lashes / 2 guard = 5 received_lashes = received_lashes / 2 guard = 6 received_lashes = received_lashes / 2 This approach helps us understand the calculation at a basic level. However, writing the same code repeatedly is not efficient. Also, we do not know how many guards there are. ## Step 2: Identifying the Repeated Pattern We can see that two operations are repeated: 1. Divide `received_lashes` by `2` . 2. Increase the guard count by `1` . For example: #python guard = guard + 1 received_lashes = received_lashes / 2 Since the same operations are repeated, we can use a while loop . Step 3: Using a While Loop guard = 0 received_lashes = 1024 while received_lashes >= 1 : received_lashes = received_lashes / 2 guard = guard + 1 print ( received_lashes ) print ( guard ) ! [ ] ( https : // dev - to - uploads . s3 . us - east - 2 . amazonaws . com / uploads / articles / x3tse2qigyuiqyeo9xpc . png ) Output 0.5 11 Explanation The value is divided by 2 repeatedly: 1024 → 512 → 256 → 128 → 64 → 32 → 16 → 8 → 4 → 2 → 1 → 0.5 The loop runs 11 times . Therefore: Number of guards = 11 Remaining value = 0.5 Step 4: What Happens if We Start with guard = 1 ? guard = 1 received_lashes = 1024 while received_lashes >= 1: received_lashes = received_lashes / 2 guard = guard + 1 print(received_lashes) print(guard) Output 0.5 12 This happens because we started counting the guards from 1 instead of 0 . is the correct and clearer approach. Correct Answer: Guards counted: 11 Final remaining value: 0.5

title: A Tiny Python Helper for Sizing Casters on Carts and Racks
author: Donyaie Charkh
summary: If you build internal tools for a warehouse, a workshop or a hospital, sooner or later someone asks a deceptively simple question: "Which casters should we order for this cart?" Getting it wrong means wheels that flat-spot in a month, bearings that seize, or a trolley nobody wants to push. The core of the answer is arithmetic, so it fits nicely in a small, testable function. Here is a version I like to keep around. The rule of thumb The common shop-floor rule is: Required capacity per caster = (equipment weight + max load) / (number of casters - 1) Why minus one? Floors are never perfectly flat. On an uneven floor or over a threshold, one caster is often barely touching the ground, so the remaining casters carry the whole load. Dividing by n - 1 builds in that margin. Then you add a safety factor for shock loads, ramps and rough handling. The code from dataclasses import dataclass @dataclass class CasterSpec : capacity_per_caster_kg : float min_wheel_diameter_mm : int note : str def size_casters ( equipment_kg : float , load_kg : float , casters : int = 4 , rough_floor : bool = False , shock : bool = False ) -> CasterSpec : if casters < 3 : raise ValueError ( "Use at least 3 casters for a stable cart" ) total = equipment_kg + load_kg per_caster = total / ( casters - 1 ) factor = 1.0 if rough_floor : factor += 0.2 if shock : factor += 0.3 capacity = round ( per_caster * factor , 1 ) # Bigger wheels roll over cracks and cables more easily. if capacity > 500 or rough_floor : diameter = 150 elif capacity > 150 : diameter = 125 else : diameter = 100 note = "polyurethane on smooth floors" if not rough_floor else "rubber or soft tread for rough floors" return CasterSpec ( capacity , diameter , note ) print ( size_casters ( equipment_kg = 60 , load_kg = 400 , casters = 4 , rough_floor = True ) ) # CasterSpec(capacity_per_caster_kg=184.0, min_wheel_diameter_mm=150, note='rubber or soft tread for rough floors') Tests keep the rule honest def test_divides_by_n_minus_one ( ) : spec = size_casters ( 0 , 300 , casters = 4 ) assert spec . capacity_per_caster_kg == 100.0 def test_rough_floor_bumps_diameter ( ) : assert size_casters ( 0 , 90 , rough_floor = True ) . min_wheel_diameter_mm == 150 What the function does not decide for you Numbers are only half the job. You still have to pick: Wheel material. Polyurethane rolls easily and protects finished floors; rubber is quieter and grips better on rough or wet ground. Swivel vs fixed layout. Two fixed at the back and two swivel at the front tracks straight on long runs; four swivels suit tight rooms. Brakes or a jack stop for anything that must stay put while people work on it. Environment. Cold rooms, ovens and washdown areas each need their own materials. For those choices, real catalogue data beats guessing. As an example, Donyaie Charkh, an industrial caster manufacturer in Iran with branches in Rasht and Tehran, publishes a practical buyer's guide for industrial wheels that walks through load, floor and mounting choices in order, and their range of refrigerator and appliance casters at https://donyaiecharkh.com/category/refrigerator-casters is a good reference for what low-profile, cold-resistant wheels look like. You can find the full catalogue on the Donyaie Charkh website . Wrap-up Wrap the arithmetic in a function, add two or three tests, and your "which casters?" conversations get shorter and more consistent. Then let the floor, the environment and a good catalogue decide the rest.

title: FastAPI: clasifica fallos de email sin reintentar a ciegas
author: Olivia Cheng
summary: En una API que envía emails, el reintento suele parecer la solución más fácil: si la entrega falla, esperamos un poco y repetimos. El problema aparece cuando tratamos igual un timeout, una dirección inválida y una bandeja temporal que todavía no ha recibido el mensaje. El sistema insiste, aumenta el ruido y al final nadie sabe qué ocurrió realmente. En proyectos con FastAPI me resulta más útil clasificar el fallo antes de decidir la siguiente acción. Así una automatización puede reintentar un problema transitorio, detenerse ante un error permanente y dejar el caso en revisión cuando falta información. Es un cambio pequeño, pero hace que las APIs sean más previsibles. El error no siempre merece otro intento Hay tres familias que conviene separar desde el principio: Transitorio: timeout, conexión reiniciada o respuesta 5xx del proveedor. Puede merecer un reintento con límite. Permanente: formato inválido, dominio inexistente o credenciales rechazadas. Repetirlo no lo arregla. Indeterminado: el proveedor aceptó la solicitud, pero la respuesta se perdió. Aquí hace falta una consulta de estado o una clave de idempotencia. El objetivo no es adivinar el futuro. Es evitar que el código convierta cualquier excepción en una orden de “hazlo otra vez”. Una función de dominio puede devolver una decisión clara: retry , stop o review . Clasifica antes de reintentar Podemos representar la decisión con un modelo pequeño. No hace falta construir un sistema de reglas enorme para empezar: from enum import StrEnum from pydantic import BaseModel class NextAction ( StrEnum ) : RETRY = "retry" STOP = "stop" REVIEW = "review" class DeliveryDecision ( BaseModel ) : action : NextAction reason : str retry_after_seconds : int | None = None def decide_delivery ( status_code : int | None , attempts : int ) -> DeliveryDecision : if attempts >= 3 : return DeliveryDecision ( action = NextAction . REVIEW , reason = "límite alcanzado" ) if status_code is None or status_code >= 500 : return DeliveryDecision ( action = NextAction . RETRY , reason = "fallo transitorio" , retry_after_seconds = 2 ** attempts , ) if status_code in { 400 , 401 , 403 , 422 } : return DeliveryDecision ( action = NextAction . STOP , reason = "fallo permanente" ) return DeliveryDecision ( action = NextAction . REVIEW , reason = "respuesta no clasificada" ) La regla importante está en el orden. Primero se comprueba el límite de intentos y después el tipo de respuesta. Si no, un proveedor que devuelve 503 puede generar una cadena de reintentos infinita. El backoff es sencillo a propósito; luego se le puede añadir un poco de jitter para que varios workers no vuelvan al mismo tiempo. Un endpoint pequeño en FastAPI La API no tiene que conocer todos los detalles del proveedor. Puede recibir el resultado normalizado de un worker y exponer la decisión para que el siguiente paso sea explícito: from fastapi import FastAPI app = FastAPI ( ) @app . post ( "/deliveries/{delivery_id}/decision" , response_model = DeliveryDecision ) def delivery_decision ( delivery_id : str , status_code : int | None = None , attempts : int = 0 ) : # En producción, delivery_id debería resolver el estado persistido. return decide_delivery ( status_code , attempts ) En producción validaría que delivery_id existe, limitaría attempts recibido por el cliente y guardaría la decisión junto al evento original. El endpoint es un ejemplo del contrato, no una invitación a confiar en datos enviados sin autenticación. También ayuda separar la entrega de la observación. Un aviso de email con contexto real necesita decir qué evento falló, qué intento era y qué acción se tomó. La interfaz que consume la API no debería recibir solo “error 500”. Registra la decisión, no solo la excepción Para depurar una automatización, guardaría al menos estos campos: delivery_id, event_id, attempt, provider_status, classification, next_action, retry_after, created_at No conviene registrar el contenido completo del mensaje ni tokens de acceso. Un identificador de evento y una razón corta suelen bastar. Si el test usa un temp org mail o un dummy e mail , la fixture debe quedar aislada del correo real y tener una caducidad conocida. En esta parte, el polling también necesita límites sanos: duración máxima, intervalo y condición de salida. Una espera que no sabe cuándo terminar es una fuga de tiempo escondida dentro del test. Pruebas para automatizaciones previsibles Las pruebas unitarias deben cubrir la tabla de decisiones, no únicamente el camino feliz: def test_timeout_retries_with_backoff ( ) : result = decide_delivery ( None , attempts = 1 ) assert result . action == NextAction . RETRY assert result . retry_after_seconds == 2 def test_invalid_address_stops ( ) : result = decide_delivery ( 422 , attempts = 0 ) assert result . action == NextAction . STOP def test_max_attempts_goes_to_review ( ) : result = decide_delivery ( 503 , attempts = 3 ) assert result . action == NextAction . REVIEW Para una prueba de integración, simularía una respuesta 503 seguida de 202 y comprobaría que solo hay dos llamadas. Después probaría un 422 y verificaría que no aparece una segunda llamada. Es facil olvidar este último caso cuando todo el entorno de pruebas responde demasiado bien. Si el flujo tiene una interfaz web, vale la pena conectar el estado backend con mensajes comprensibles. Un estado “revisar” es mejor que un spinner eterno; este tipo de detalle también aparece al diseñar avisos de email con contexto real . Para comprobar la bandeja, puedes aplicar polling de inbox con límites sanos . Q&A: dudas habituales ¿Debo reintentar todos los errores 5xx? No necesariamente. Un 5xx suele ser transitorio, pero el proveedor puede estar rechazando una operación por saturación o por una cuota. Usa un máximo de intentos, backoff y una ruta de revisión. Si existe un encabezado Retry-After , úsalo dentro de un límite razonable. ¿Qué hago si no recibo respuesta? Trátalo como indeterminado. Antes de enviar otra vez, consulta el estado con un identificador idempotente. Duplicar un email porque se perdió la respuesta es peor que tardar unos segundos en confirmar. Checklist de implementación Define las categorías transitorio, permanente e indeterminado. Pon un límite de intentos fuera del proveedor. Devuelve una acción explícita: reintentar, detener o revisar. Registra evento, intento y decisión sin guardar datos innecesarios. Añade backoff y, cuando aplique, Retry-After . Prueba una secuencia 5xx → éxito y otra con error permanente. Establece un timeout para cada polling y para el flujo completo. La automatización de email no necesita más reintentos, sino mejores decisiones. Cuando FastAPI expone un contrato pequeño y cada fallo deja evidencia suficiente, los workers pueden recuperarse sin ocultar los casos que necesitan atención humana.

title: JavaScript Closures Explained with Simple Examples
author: Lavkush Kumar
summary: Originally published on CodingCush . A closure is a function that remembers the variables from the place where it was created, even after that place has finished running. That sentence explains a lot of JavaScript behaviour that feels like magic at first: counters that keep counting, buttons that remember their own value, and helpers that carry private data. In this guide you will learn what a closure really is, how lexical scope makes it work, and how to use closures in real code, with every example tested in Node.js. What Is a Closure, in Plain Words? Imagine a backpack. When a function is created inside another function, JavaScript quietly packs the variables around it into a backpack and hands that backpack to the inner function. Wherever the inner function goes later, the backpack goes with it. The inner function can open the backpack and use those variables at any time. The formal definition is not much scarier. A closure is the combination of a function and the environment in which it was declared. The MDN guide to closures puts it this way: a closure gives a function access to its outer scope, and closures are created every time a function is created. You have probably written dozens already without knowing the name. Step 1: See the Smallest Possible Closure Start with an outer function that creates a variable and an inner function that uses it: function greet ( ) { const name = "Asha" ; function sayHello ( ) { console . log ( "Hello, " + name ) ; } sayHello ( ) ; } greet ( ) ; Expected output: Hello, Asha Here sayHello has no variable called name of its own. It borrows name from greet , the function it was born inside. This works because of lexical scope : JavaScript decides where a variable comes from by looking at where the code is written, not where it is called from. If the variable is not found in the inner function, JavaScript looks one level out, then another, until it reaches the global scope. This example is a closure in its simplest clothing, but nothing surprising happens yet, because sayHello runs while greet is still alive. The real trick appears when the inner function outlives the outer one. Step 2: A Function That Returns a Function Now return the inner function instead of calling it straight away: function makeGreeter ( ) { const name = "Asha" ; return function ( ) { console . log ( "Hello, " + name ) ; } ; } const greetAsha = makeGreeter ( ) ; greetAsha ( ) ; Expected output: Hello, Asha Look closely at the last two lines. makeGreeter() has finished running. In many languages, its local variable name would now be gone, like chalk wiped off a board. But greetAsha() still prints "Asha". The returned function kept its backpack. That memory is the closure. Scope behaviour depends on how you declare variables, which is why the difference in our guide to var vs let vs const in JavaScript and what the difference is matters so much here: closures capture variables declared with any of them, but let and const give each block its own copy, as you will see in the loop example below. Step 3: Build a Counter (The Classic Interview Example) Here is the example interviewers love, because it shows closures doing real work: keeping state private. function makeCounter ( start ) { let count = start ; return function ( ) { count = count + 1 ; return count ; } ; } const counter = makeCounter ( 10 ) ; console . log ( counter ( ) ) ; console . log ( counter ( ) ) ; console . log ( counter ( ) ) ; Expected output (tested with Node.js): 11 12 13 Three things are happening. First, count survives between calls, because the returned function closes over it. Second, nobody outside can touch count directly; that is free privacy, no classes needed. Third, every call to makeCounter creates a fresh backpack, so makeCounter(100) counts from 100 without disturbing the first counter. The real output of the examples in this article, run with Node.js: the counter prints 11, 12, 13, the adder factory prints 7 and 12, and the loop test shows var printing 3 three times while let prints 0, 1, 2. Step 4: Function Factories with makeAdder A closure can also remember a setting, which turns a function into a small factory: function makeAdder ( x ) { return function ( y ) { return x + y ; } ; } const add5 = makeAdder ( 5 ) ; const add10 = makeAdder ( 10 ) ; console . log ( add5 ( 2 ) ) ; console . log ( add10 ( 2 ) ) ; Expected output (tested with Node.js): 7 12 add5 and add10 share the same code but carry different backpacks: one remembers x as 5, the other as 10. This pattern sits behind a lot of real code: event handlers that remember which item they belong to, middleware that remembers its options, and callbacks in general. That is also why closures pair naturally with asynchronous code, as our guide to JavaScript promises and async/await explained with simple examples shows: the function you hand over today brings its variables with it tomorrow. Step 5: The Famous Loop Problem (and the let Fix) This example has embarrassed many of us in interviews, so meet it here first, in friendly conditions: for ( var i = 0 ; i < 3 ; i ++ ) { setTimeout ( function ( ) { console . log ( "var" , i ) ; } , 0 ) ; } for ( let j = 0 ; j < 3 ; j ++ ) { setTimeout ( function ( ) { console . log ( "let" , j ) ; } , 10 ) ; } Expected output (tested with Node.js): var 3 var 3 var 3 let 0 let 1 let 2 Why does var print 3 three times? All three callbacks close over the same variable i , and by the time the timers fire, the loop has finished and i is 3. With let , each round gets its own fresh j , so each callback remembers a different backpack. Same closures, different scope rules. Where Closures Show Up in Real Projects Use case What the closure remembers Click handlers Which item, tab or button the handler belongs to Counters and ID generators The last number used, kept private Function factories A setting such as a tax rate, a prefix or a limit Debounce and throttle helpers The timer ID and the last call time Module pattern Private data that only the returned methods can reach React hooks such as useState The current state value between renders Closures also power the handlers you attach when you change a page by hand, as in our guide to what the DOM is in JavaScript, explained simply : every click callback remembers the elements and values from its birthplace. One honest warning: a closure keeps its variables alive while the function is reachable, so a forgotten listener can hold on to a large object. Long-lived closures deserve housekeeping, like anything else. Common Mistakes and Troubleshooting Expecting a fresh copy with var in a loop. You saw the output above: three callbacks, one shared variable. Use let in the loop, or pass the value into an inner function straight away. Thinking the closure copies the value. A closure captures the variable, not a photograph of it. If the outer code changes the variable later, the inner function sees the new value. This is a feature for counters and a surprise for everyone else, once. Creating closures in hot loops without noticing. Defining a function inside a loop creates a new closure each round. Usually fine, but in tight loops over thousands of items, define the function once outside and pass values in. Confusing closures with scope itself. Scope is the rule book that decides which variables a piece of code can see. A closure is what you get when a function keeps access to that scope after the outer function returns. The MDN functions guide is a good next read if the rule book still feels fuzzy. Frequently Asked Questions Is every function in JavaScript a closure? Practically, yes. Every function is created with a link to the scope around it. The word closure is usually used when that link becomes interesting, most often when an inner function is returned or passed as a callback and used after the outer function ends. What is the difference between a closure and scope? Scope is the set of variables a piece of code can access, decided by where the code is written. A closure is a function bundled together with the variables from its birthplace scope, so it can keep using them later. Do closures waste memory? They keep the captured variables alive while the function is reachable, which is exactly what counters and handlers need. Problems start only when closures outlive their purpose, for example listeners that are never removed on long-lived pages. How do I practise closures? Write the counter and the adder factory from this article without looking, predict each output before you run it, then try the loop example with var and let. Predicting outputs is the fastest way to make the idea stick. Conclusion A closure is a function plus the variables it was born next to. Return the function, hand it to a timer or a click handler, and those variables travel with it, privately and reliably. Once you see the backpack, counters, factories, callbacks and even React hooks all start to look like the same friendly idea wearing different clothes.

title: How to Add Booking to a Next.js App With a REST API (2026)
author: Stan
summary: Originally published on opencals.com . The original stays updated; check it for the latest version. Adding a booking page to a Next.js app looks like a weekend project until you start it. The UI is the easy part. The hard part is everything the calendar needs to know before it can show a single open slot: which staff are working, how long the service takes, what's already booked, how much buffer to leave between appointments, and whether two people can hold the same slot at once. That logic is where booking projects quietly turn into month-long ones. This guide takes the other path. Instead of building the scheduling engine yourself, you call a booking API for the availability, cart, and payment logic, and you keep full control of the Next.js frontend. I built Opencals as exactly that kind of API, so the code here uses it — but the shape of the problem is the same whichever backend you pick, and I'll flag the parts that are universal. Key takeaway The frontend of a booking flow is a few forms and a calendar grid. The backend is real-time availability across staff, services, and existing bookings — plus payments. Calling a booking API lets you own the first part and hand off the second. What "add booking" actually involves Before any code, it helps to name the pieces. A working booking flow has four moving parts, and most half-finished projects stall because they underestimated one of them. 1. A service catalog What can be booked — a 60-minute session, a color treatment, a group class — each with its own duration, price, and the staff who can deliver it. This is your booking homepage data. 2. Real-time availability Given a service and a date range, which slots are actually open? This has to account for existing bookings, staff hours, buffer time, and multi-staff conflicts. It is the single hardest piece to build well. 3. A cart and checkout Holding a slot while the customer enters details and pays, then confirming the booking only if payment succeeds. Slots are a scarce resource, so this needs to be race-safe. 4. Post-booking management Confirmation, reminders, and letting customers reschedule or cancel without emailing you. Easy to skip on day one, painful to add later. If you build all four yourself, you're writing a scheduling engine. If you call an API, you're wiring four typed methods into React components. This guide does the second. Prerequisites You need a Next.js 14+ app using the App Router, Node 18+, and a booking API key. With Opencals that's a private storefront key (prefixed spk_ ), created in the dashboard under Users → your user → API Keys; any booking API will have an equivalent. Install the SDK: npm i @opencals/storefront-sdk Then set the key in your environment. Keep it server-side — a private storefront key can create real bookings, so it does not belong in client bundles. # .env.local OPENCALS_API_KEY = spk_your_key_here Why server-side Anything that creates a booking or a payment should run in a Route Handler or Server Action, never in a client component. The browser calls your Next.js API routes; your routes call the booking API with the secret key. This is the same pattern you'd use for a Stripe secret key. Step 1 — Initialise the SDK once Create a small module that configures the client. setupOpencals sets up the SDK's shared client, so you call it once and every service call after that uses the key. Import this module at the top of any server file that calls the API. // lib/opencals.ts — import from server code only import { setupOpencals } from "@opencals/storefront-sdk" ; import { nextBuyerIp } from "@opencals/storefront-sdk/next" ; setupOpencals ( { apiKey : process . env . OPENCALS_API_KEY , // spk_… buyerIp : nextBuyerIp , throwOnError : true , // failed calls throw OpencalsApiError instead of returning { error } } ) ; nextBuyerIp forwards each visitor's IP on sign-in, cart and checkout calls, so the API rate-limits per visitor instead of treating your server as one very busy customer. It skips GET requests on purpose, so your cached pages stay static. If you prefer raw fetch over an SDK, the same call is a GET with the key in an X-Api-Key header — the SDK just gives you typed responses. Both work; typing saves you from guessing the shape of a nested availability object at 11pm. curl https://api.opencals.com/storefront/products \ -H "X-Api-Key: spk_your_key" Step 2 — List services on a Server Component The App Router lets you fetch on the server and stream HTML, which is ideal for a service catalog — it's public data, good for SEO, and doesn't need to be interactive. // app/book/page.tsx import "@/lib/opencals" ; import { ProductService } from "@opencals/storefront-sdk" ; import { ServiceCard } from "./service-card" ; export default async function BookPage ( ) { const { data : page } = await ProductService . list ( { query : { status : [ "active" ] , take : 50 } , throwOnError : true , } ) ; return ( < main className = "grid gap-4" > { page . data . map ( ( service ) => ( < ServiceCard key = { service . id } service = { service } /> ) ) } </ main > ) ; } The list comes back as { data, meta } , fully typed. Each service carries its price (in minor units), duration (seconds), beforeGap / afterGap buffers and a variants array, each variant with its own price and duration. formatPrice and formatDuration from the SDK turn those into display strings. You render, you don't compute. Step 3 — Fetch real-time availability This is the endpoint that would have taken you weeks to write. You pass a service and a date, optionally a staff member or location, and you get back the slots that are open right now. // app/api/availability/route.ts (Route Handler) import { NextRequest , NextResponse } from "next/server" ; import "@/lib/opencals" ; import { ProductService } from "@opencals/storefront-sdk" ; export async function GET ( req : NextRequest ) { const { searchParams } = new URL ( req . url ) ; const { data : slots } = await ProductService . getCurrentAvailabilities ( { path : { productId : searchParams . get ( "productId" ) ! } , query : { date : searchParams . get ( "date" ) ! , // YYYY-MM-DD staffMemberId : searchParams . get ( "staffMemberId" ) ?? undefined , timezone : "Europe/Warsaw" , // your store's timezone } , } ) ; return NextResponse . json ( { slots } ) ; } Each slot is { fromDate, fromTime, toDate, toTime, staffMemberIds, attendees, maxAttendees } , and the list already leaves out times that are booked, outside staff hours, or too close to another appointment given the service's buffers. Your calendar component fetches this route when the user picks a date and renders whatever comes back — no client-side conflict math. For a month view, getCurrentAvailabilitiesMerged returns the broad open windows so you can grey out full days. The universal part Every booking backend worth using exposes an availability endpoint like this. If a tool only gives you raw calendar events and expects you to compute open slots yourself, you haven't offloaded the hard part — you've just moved it. Availability calculation is the feature to evaluate first. Step 4 — Hold the slot with a cart A slot is a scarce resource. Between "customer clicked 2pm" and "customer paid," you don't want someone else grabbing it, and you don't want to create a real booking that might never be paid for. A cart holds the slot for a short window: you create (or reuse) a cart, then create the appointment inside it. // app/api/cart/route.ts import { NextRequest , NextResponse } from "next/server" ; import { cookies } from "next/headers" ; import "@/lib/opencals" ; import { AppointmentService , CartService } from "@opencals/storefront-sdk" ; export async function POST ( req : NextRequest ) { const { slot } = await req . json ( ) ; // one slot from step 3 const jar = await cookies ( ) ; const { data : cart } = await CartService . createOrGet ( { headers : { "X-Cart-Id" : jar . get ( "cartId" ) ? . value ?? "" } , } ) ; await AppointmentService . create ( { body : { slot : { productId : slot . productId , fromDate : slot . fromDate , fromTime : slot . fromTime , toDate : slot . toDate , toTime : slot . toTime , } , numberOfAttendees : 1 , cartId : cart . id , } , } ) ; jar . set ( "cartId" , cart . id , { httpOnly : true , sameSite : "lax" } ) ; return NextResponse . json ( { cartId : cart . id } ) ; } The cart ID lives in an httpOnly cookie, and every cart and checkout call names its cart with the X-Cart-Id header. Times are UTC. If two people try to hold the same slot at the same moment, one succeeds and the other gets a clear error, so your UI can say "someone just took that time" instead of double-booking. Step 5 — Check out and pay Checkout turns a held cart into a paid booking in two server calls with the card confirmation in between. start attaches the customer, re-checks the cart and creates the payment; the browser confirms the card with Stripe; submit places the order. // app/api/checkout/start/route.ts import { NextRequest , NextResponse } from "next/server" ; import { cookies } from "next/headers" ; import "@/lib/opencals" ; import { CheckoutService } from "@opencals/storefront-sdk" ; export async function POST ( req : NextRequest ) { const { email , firstName , lastName } = await req . json ( ) ; const cartId = ( await cookies ( ) ) . get ( "cartId" ) ! . value ; const { data : checkout } = await CheckoutService . start ( { headers : { "X-Cart-Id" : cartId } , body : { provider : "stripe" , customer : { kind : "new" , email , firstName , lastName } } , } ) ; // The browser needs these to mount a Stripe Payment Element. return NextResponse . json ( { clientSecret : checkout . clientSecret , publishableKey : checkout . publishableKey , stripeAccountId : checkout . stripeAccountId , } ) ; } // app/api/checkout/submit/route.ts — called after stripe.confirmPayment() succeeds in the browser import { NextRequest , NextResponse } from "next/server" ; import { cookies } from "next/headers" ; import "@/lib/opencals" ; import { CheckoutService } from "@opencals/storefront-sdk" ; export async function POST ( req : NextRequest ) { const { paymentIntentId } = await req . json ( ) ; const cartId = ( await cookies ( ) ) . get ( "cartId" ) ! . value ; const { data : result } = await CheckoutService . submit ( { headers : { "X-Cart-Id" : cartId } , body : { stripePaymentIntentId : paymentIntentId } , } ) ; return NextResponse . json ( result ) ; } The Stripe publishable key comes back from start , from the store's own Stripe connection, so there is no Stripe key to configure in your app. If the card wasn't authorised (declined, 3-D Secure not finished), submit answers 402 with the code PAYMENT_NOT_AUTHORIZED , no order is placed and the cart is untouched, so the customer can try again. A second start or submit on the same cart while one is running gets CHECKOUT_IN_PROGRESS instead of a duplicate order. The slot only becomes a real booking once the payment is authorised. Step 6 — Let customers manage their own bookings The reschedule-and-cancel flow is the one teams skip first and regret most, because without it every change becomes a support message. These calls run as the signed-in customer: AuthService.signIn returns an accessToken , and you send it as a Bearer token next to your store key, so the customer only sees and touches their own bookings. // server code, with the customer's accessToken from AuthService.signIn import "@/lib/opencals" ; import { AppointmentService } from "@opencals/storefront-sdk" ; const asCustomer = { Authorization : `Bearer ${accessToken}` } ; const { data : upcoming } = await AppointmentService . list ( { headers : asCustomer , query : { status : [ "scheduled" , "pending" ] , orderBy : "from" , order : "ASC" } , } ) ; await AppointmentService . reschedule ( { headers : asCustomer , path : { appointmentId } , body : { slot : newSlot } , // a slot from getCurrentAvailabilities, fetched with excludeAppointmentId } ) ; Pass excludeAppointmentId when you fetch availability for a reschedule, so the appointment's own slot isn't shown as taken. The store's reschedule and cancel windows still apply. Wire these into an account page and the reschedule requests that used to hit your inbox now resolve themselves. Putting it together The full flow, from the frontend's point of view, is six typed calls in five steps: 1. List services ProductService.list() → render the catalog on a Server Component. 2. Check availability ProductService.getCurrentAvailabilities() → the open slots for a date, computed server-side. 3. Hold the slot CartService.createOrGet() + AppointmentService.create() → the chosen slot is held in a cart while the customer checks out. 4. Start checkout CheckoutService.start() → the customer is attached and a payment is created for the browser to confirm. 5. Place the order CheckoutService.submit() → the held slot becomes a real, paid booking. Everything hard about scheduling — the availability math, the race conditions, the payment-to-booking handoff — lives behind those calls. Your Next.js app stays a frontend: forms, a calendar grid, and route handlers that proxy to the API with your secret key. When not to use an API for this Honest caveat, because not every project needs this. If you're a solo consultant booking 1:1 calls and you don't take payment up front, a hosted tool like Calendly is simpler and you shouldn't build anything. An API earns its keep when you need a custom-branded flow, multiple staff or locations, payments at booking, or booking embedded inside a product you already own. That's when owning the frontend while renting the backend is the right trade — and the links below cover the endpoint surface, the architecture, and the typed SDK. Where to go from here Booking API guide : The endpoint-level reference: auth model, core routes, and the full booking flow in raw REST. Booking SDK : The typed TypeScript SDK used in this guide — services, availability, cart, and checkout end to end. Headless booking system : The architecture behind building a custom booking frontend on any stack. Opencals for developers : API docs, the OpenAPI spec, and how to get a storefront key. Build a booking website : Three approaches compared, from no-code to a fully custom build. Frequently asked questions Can I add booking to Next.js without a third-party API? Yes, but you're then building a scheduling engine: real-time availability across staff and services, buffer logic, race-safe slot holding, and payment-to-booking handoff. For a single service with no payments that's doable in a weekend. For anything with multiple staff, locations, or paid bookings, the availability and concurrency logic is where most of the effort goes — which is what an API removes. Where do I keep the booking API key in Next.js? Server-side only — in an environment variable read by Route Handlers or Server Actions. A storefront key can create real bookings and charges, so it must never ship in a client bundle. The browser calls your own Next.js API routes; those routes call the booking API with the secret key. Does this work with the App Router and Server Components? Yes. Public reads like the service catalog fit Server Components and stream as HTML, which is good for SEO. Anything that mutates — cart, checkout, reschedule — goes in Route Handlers or Server Actions so the secret key stays on the server. How is a booking API different from a calendar API like Google Calendar? A calendar API stores and returns events. A booking API computes availability — it knows service durations, staff assignments, buffers, and existing bookings, and returns the slots a customer can actually book. With a calendar API you'd still have to write all of that logic yourself on top of raw events. Can customers reschedule or cancel on their own? Yes. The customer signs in through the API (AuthService.signIn returns an access token), and your server calls AppointmentService.list, reschedule and cancel with that token as a Bearer header next to the store key, so each customer only sees their own bookings. The store's reschedule and cancel windows still apply. Wire them into an account page and the change requests you'd otherwise answer by email resolve themselves.

title: 505,000 Chinese characters, 3 MB APK: shipping a classical text as an offline reader
author: RUNZEAI
summary: I have been writing a commentary on the Yijing (Book of Changes) for a while. It ended up at 72 sections, 505,000 non-whitespace Chinese characters, and 704 A4 pages. At that point the interesting question stopped being "what does it say" and became "how does somebody actually read the thing" — on a phone, on a train, with no network. This post is the build log: one Markdown source, four deliverables, and the parts that broke. Repo: q1z2q3-debug/daokedao-yijing · Reading site: q1z2q3-debug.github.io/daokedao-yijing The shape of the problem One source of truth ( book/*.md ), four outputs that must never drift: Output How Size Reading page Markdown → pandoc → one self-contained HTML 1.75 MB Print book Chromium print-to-PDF, segmented then merged 29 MB / 704 pp Offline reader The same HTML inside a WebView shell 3.0 MB APK Indexed site 70 pages generated from the same HTML 4.5 MB The rule I settled on: the HTML is the artifact, everything else derives from it. The APK is not a second implementation — it is that exact file plus fonts. Step 1 — make the HTML actually self-contained The reading page was originally pulling a webfont from a CDN. Fine online, useless on a plane. So the build step rewrites the page and inlines a subset: pyftsubset NotoSerifSC-Regular.otf \ --text-file=charset.txt \ --unicodes= "U+4DC0-4DFF,U+2630-2640" \ --flavor=woff2 --layout-features= '*' Two details worth stealing: Build the charset from the book, not from a guess. I extracted every codepoint that actually appears (3,100 of them) instead of shipping a 20 MB full CJK font. Two weights, ~2.5 MB total. Do not forget the symbol blocks. The Yijing uses ䷀ – ䷿ (U+4DC0–U+4DFF) for hexagrams and ☰ – ☷ for trigrams. A CJK-only subset silently renders them as tofu boxes. They are not in the CJK Unified Ideographs block, so a charset scraped from \u4e00-\u9fff misses them. Result: zero external references left in the file , fonts embedded as base64, 1.75 MB, opens from file:// with the network switched off. Step 2 — an APK without Gradle Android Studio was not available in the environment, and honestly a WebView shell does not need it. Six steps: aapt2 compile → res.zip aapt2 link → resources + R.java + assets + manifest javac → classes d8 → classes.dex zipalign → 4-byte aligned apksigner → v1/v2/v3 Two gotchas that cost me time: platform-34_r03.zip 404s. The build-tools_r34-linux.zip is fine, but the matching platform package for that revision is gone. I used platform-35_r02.zip for android.jar with targetSdk 34 in the manifest. Works. Test mobile layout with a mobile viewport, not a narrow desktop window. Chromium with --window-size=420 ignores , so the page renders at desktop width and gets clipped on the right — a fake overflow bug. Playwright with is_mobile=True showed scrollWidth == 390 and no overflow at all. I nearly rewrote CSS that was already correct. The manifest has zero permissions — not even INTERNET : and the shell adds setBlockNetworkLoads(true) so a stray in the content cannot phone home either. Version code 15000 = version 1.50.0 encoded, so the next release is 15100 and installs over it with the same signing key. Step 3 — 70 pages, because one 1.75 MB page ranks for nothing This is the part that matters if you ever publish a long text on the web. A single page containing the entire book is a terrible search target: one , no <meta name="description"> , no canonical, and nothing to rank for a query like "未济卦 解读". So the site build splits the same HTML on its <h1> boundaries and wraps each section in a template: /p/64-weiji/ — one directory per hexagram, canonical URL, 50–75 character description taken from the section's own opening line prev/next links, so crawlers can walk the whole chain from any entry point sitemap.xml (72 URLs), robots.txt , llms.txt (a plain-text summary for AI crawlers) JSON-LD: Article per page, Book + hasPart on the landing page one 1200×630 OG image, generated deterministically with Pillow The whole generator is ~250 lines of Python and runs in under a second: python3 scripts/build-site.py # 70 pages + sitemap + robots + llms.txt Two things I would do differently next time: Generate descriptions from the text, not from headings. My first pass concatenated the heading, a byline, and the first paragraph — producing junk like 第 64 卦：未济。下 经｜未济 润泽说易 到不了岸… . Pulling the section's opening pull-quote fixed it. Keep the generator in the repo. The pages are build output; if the source moves, the site must be one command away from being correct again, not a folder of hand-edited HTML. Step 4 — release plumbing GitHub release assets are picky: Non-ASCII asset names get mangled. 道可道-易传-1.50.0.apk arrived as -.-1.50.0.apk . Use ASCII names; keep the Chinese title in the release body. Uploads need Accept: application/vnd.github+json on uploads.github.com , otherwise you get an HTML 400 page and no explanation. A v* tag workflow re-attaches the PDF, APK and prompt PDF automatically, so a release is a tag, not fifteen manual clicks. What I'd tell someone starting the same thing Pick one artifact as the source of truth and derive everything from it. A book, a PDF and an APK that are maintained separately will disagree within two releases. Subset fonts from the actual corpus, and check the symbol blocks. If the text is long, publish it as many pages with real descriptions. One giant page is invisible. Zero permissions is a feature. A reading app that cannot reach the network is a reading app that cannot leak, and users notice. The book is CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. If you want the APK, it is on the releases page — 3 MB, no permissions, works in airplane mode.

title: How to fix "SPF permerror: too many DNS lookups"
author: Hanzala Rasool
summary: SPF has a hard limit: checking your record may take no more than 10 DNS lookups . Go over it and the result is permerror , which many receivers treat as a failed SPF check, so your mail is more likely to land in spam. It usually creeps up on you as you add more services that send email for you. What counts towards the 10 Counts: include: , a , mx , ptr , exists: and redirect= Doesn't count: ip4: , ip6: and all Nested lookups count too. include:_spf.google.com is one lookup, but Google's record includes others, and those count against your 10 as well. Find what's using your lookups Look at your current record: nslookup -type=txt yourdomain.com Count every include , a , mx , ptr and exists , then repeat for each included domain. Or paste your domain into a checker that does it for you, like this free SPF & DMARC check . If the top level is already close to 10, the includes inside it almost certainly push you over. Five ways to get under the limit Remove services you no longer use. Old newsletter tools and CRMs are the usual culprits. Replace a and mx with ip4: if your own servers have fixed IP addresses. IP addresses don't use lookups. Remove ptr . It's deprecated and slow anyway. Send marketing mail from a subdomain , such as news.yourdomain.com , with its own SPF record. Each domain gets its own 10 lookups. Flatten carefully. Replacing an include with the IP addresses it contains saves lookups, but if the provider changes its IPs your SPF silently breaks. Only flatten with a tool that keeps it updated. Don't forget DKIM DMARC passes if either SPF or DKIM passes and aligns with your domain. Setting up DKIM for every service that sends as you makes SPF less critical, and some services can't be added to SPF at all without going over the limit. Quick end-to-end test: send yourself an email in Gmail, open it, choose Show original , and look for PASS next to SPF, DKIM and DMARC.
